title: Metrics Monitoring and Alerting
oneLine: Collect labeled time series, control cardinality, store compressed samples by time, query through downsampled tiers, and alert on SLO impact rather than every noisy spike.
opening: I would separate collection, ingestion, time-series storage, query, and alerting. Services expose metrics for pull-based collection where possible; agents or gateways accept push for short-lived jobs and external environments. Collectors discover targets, scrape in parallel, apply relabeling/cardinality limits, and route series by a stable hash of metric plus labels to replicated ingestion shards. Samples are buffered in a WAL, compressed into time blocks, indexed by labels, and downsampled into longer-retention tiers. The query layer fans out by time/series and caches common dashboards. Alert rules run independently, group and deduplicate incidents, support silences, and use multi-window burn-rate checks for SLOs. Raw high-cardinality events belong in logs/traces, not metrics.
ask: Infrastructure/application/business metrics—and are logs/traces out of scope?
How many active series, samples/sec, labels, and retention tiers?
What alert latency, availability, and query patterns?
scale: Active series = metric names × unique label combinations; cardinality can explode before sample QPS looks large.
Retention example: raw 7 days, 1-minute 30 days, hourly one year—derive from use cases and cost.
Compression is effective because timestamps and values are delta-encoded within a series.

decisions.default: Pull for long-lived services; push gateway/agent for short-lived or inaccessible targets.
decisions.why: Pull centralizes scheduling, target health, and backpressure.
decisions.switch: Pure push for edge/IoT where inbound connectivity is impossible, with strict tenant quotas.

decisions.default: Hash full label set so all samples for a series reach one ingest owner/replica set.
decisions.why: It enables ordered compression and avoids cross-shard writes for one series.
decisions.switch: Query layer must fan out across shards for broad aggregations.

decisions.default: Alert on symptoms/SLO burn and actionable saturation; ticket low-urgency causes.
decisions.why: Thresholding every metric creates fatigue and hides real incidents.
decisions.switch: Hard invariant/security alerts may page immediately independent of SLO.

decisions.default: Raw hot blocks, downsampled warm tiers, object-store cold retention.
decisions.why: Most long-range queries do not need per-second resolution.
decisions.switch: Keep immutable raw samples longer for regulated evidence only when justified.

deepDives.title: Cardinality governance
points: Never use unbounded user/order/request IDs as labels.
Set per-tenant series budgets and reject/drop with visible telemetry.
Provide top-cardinality diagnostics and label allowlists.

deepDives.title: Alert lifecycle
points: Rule evaluation produces instances; group related labels, dedupe repeats, inhibit downstream symptoms, and honor silences.
Persist state so restarts do not resend every alert.
Multi-window burn rate catches both fast and slow SLO consumption.

deepDives.title: High availability
points: Scrape with controlled replicas and deduplicate samples or partition target ownership.
Replicate WAL/blocks and keep alert evaluators redundant with ownership leases.
Monitoring its own failure requires an independent dead-man signal.

failures.response: Admission guard, quotas, relabel/drop rules, emergency denylist, and identify offending deployment.
Bound scrape concurrency, drop/skip stale cycles explicitly, scale by target ownership, and expose scrape age.
Grouping, dedupe, inhibition, rate limits, incident aggregation, and escalation policy.

failures.risk: Monitoring backend outage hides production outage
failures.response: Replicated control/data plane, local buffering, external synthetic checks, and dead-man alert through an independent channel.

questions.q: Why are user IDs bad metric labels?
questions.a: They create one time series per user, exploding index/memory and query cost. Put high-cardinality identity in logs/traces and aggregate metrics by bounded dimensions.

questions.q: How do you store time series efficiently?
questions.a: Group samples by series and time block, delta-encode timestamps/values, write compressed immutable blocks, keep a label index, and compact/downsample older data.

It compares current error-budget consumption to the rate that would exhaust the budget. Pair a fast window with a longer confirmation window to catch severe and sustained failures with fewer false pages.

questions.q: How do you avoid duplicate samples from HA collectors?
questions.a: Assign exclusive target ownership with leases or ingest replicas carrying replica labels and deduplicate by timestamp/series at query/compaction.

mistakes: Treating metrics, logs, and traces as interchangeable
Building monitoring with no independent liveness check
seniorSignal: Lead with cardinality economics and alert quality. Explain the write-optimized TSDB path, retention/downsampling, HA semantics, and why observability must degrade predictably.
implementation: OpenTelemetry/Prometheus collection; service discovery and relabeling
WAL + compressed time blocks, with object-store long-term backend
Alertmanager-style grouping, inhibition, silence, and multi-window SLO rules
